Keep the explicit row 40px tall and make the extra row 60px tall.

quizTarget: Which property moves the whole horizontal track group into unused container space here?
reasoning: Justify-content aligns the grid tracks; justify-items aligns each item inside its area.

essentialSupport.fact: Item alignment moves an item inside its grid area. Content alignment moves the track group inside the container when free space exists.

The HTML supplies the elements; CSS supplies their presentation. This small fixture uses horizontal writing and left-to-right direction. ```html
One
``` ```css .demo { writing-mode: horizontal-tb; direction: ltr; } .grid { display: grid; width: 240px; height: 120px; grid-template-columns: 100px; grid-template-rows: 60px; justify-items: center; align-items: center; justify-content: start; align-content: start; } .item { width: 40px; height: 20px; } ```

justify-items: center centers the item along the inline axis inside its 100px area; align-items: center centers it along the block axis inside its 60px area. justify-content: start and align-content: start keep that track group at the container’s start. Here horizontal writing and LTR make inline start the left edge.

Use items alignment for cards inside cells; use content alignment for a compact grid inside a larger panel. Fixed tracks leave free space in this fixture; expanding fractional tracks may leave no space for content distribution.
Center the item within its area while keeping the track group at the top-left start.

quizTarget: If --ink is present as 12px, does the fallback teal repair this color value?
reasoning: A var fallback handles missing/invalid variable substitution, not every type error after substitution.

essentialSupport.fact: var(--ink, teal) substitutes the custom property --ink when it has a usable variable value; if it is missing, the fallback teal is substituted. A present value can still be invalid for the receiving property.

The first argument is the custom-property name; the comma starts the fallback. Here --ink is absent, so color receives teal. If --ink is defined as 12px, var substitutes 12px: that is invalid for color. The browser does not then retry the earlier purple declaration or the teal fallback. For this inherited property the result inherits navy from the parent. This is invalidity at computed-value time, after the cascade chose the declaration.

The supplied HTML is separate from the CSS. ```html

Keep the route readable

``` ```css .theme { color: navy; } .note { color: purple; color: var(--ink, teal); } ```

Give the note a teal fallback when --ink is missing. Keep the parent navy and the earlier purple declaration to expose the difference. quizTarget: If the condition tests an invalid display value, does the browser remove the base block layout?
reasoning: Conditional rules add to the cascade when their condition succeeds; they do not erase the fallback.

essentialSupport.fact: @supports tests whether the browser accepts a CSS declaration. Start with a usable ordinary layout, then enhance it when a feature is supported. Acceptance does not certify a complete accessible design or absence of rendering bugs.

@supports (display: grid) encloses rules inside braces. The condition asks about the property-value pair, not whether a particular element currently uses it. CSS.supports in the supplied check is test infrastructure for comparing the browser’s answer, not learner JavaScript to write. An invented value makes this condition false; the base rule still applies.
Keep the content usable as blocks and switch to two grid columns only under the supported declaration.

quizTarget: With duration set to zero, does adding muted stop changing the final opacity?
reasoning: The class rule supplies the final state independently from how the change is animated.

essentialSupport.fact: A transition animates a change between old and new property values. It does not create the state change itself. Here adding the muted class changes opacity; the transition smooths that change when motion is allowed.

transition: opacity 0.08s linear names the property, duration in seconds, and constant-speed timing. opacity: 0.4 makes the whole button partly transparent; it does not disable its action. The reduced-motion media query sets the duration to zero when the person requests reduced motion. The supplied test adds the class, waits for actual animations to finish, checks the endpoint, and removes the class; you only write CSS.

Animate only the opacity change, keep the native button, and provide the zero-duration reduced-motion alternative. Supplied checks inspect the authored contract and may temporarily change a value to compare the stated behavior; temporary values are restored. quizTarget: If you set only color-scheme: dark, does your explicit white author background automatically become dark?
reasoning: Native scheme participation and explicit author colors are related but distinct contracts.

essentialSupport.fact: prefers-color-scheme asks about the person’s light/dark preference. color-scheme tells the browser which scheme an element supports, helping native controls use an appropriate appearance. It does not automatically recolor every author background or text rule.

The base panel is explicitly light. The dark media branch changes both authored colors and the color-scheme value. The input keeps its native behavior. Checks verify the currently active browser preference only; this preview does not switch operating-system settings. High-contrast/forced-color mechanics are a separate topic, and meaning must not depend on color alone.
Provide explicit readable light colors and a dark-preference alternative while allowing native controls to use the corresponding scheme.

quizTarget: Does narrowing the browser window automatically activate @media print?
reasoning: A viewport-size query and a print-medium query ask different questions.

essentialSupport.fact: @media print supplies styles for printed output or print preview. A screen toolbar can be useful on screen but waste space on paper. Keep the report itself in the document and hide only screen-only controls in print.

The media type print is not a narrow viewport query. display: none inside this print branch removes the toolbar’s print layout space; outside print, its ordinary rule remains. Explicit dark text and an uncolored background can improve legibility, but exact page breaks, margins, color reproduction and printer settings still vary. This lesson is a local companion: the app does not render or grade print output.
Save the complete local page and stylesheet below, open the HTML in a browser, and compare the normal page with Print Preview. No printing or purchase is needed.

quizTarget: If .notice is misspelled .notices, should increasing its specificity fix this page?
reasoning: A selector that matches nothing contributes no declarations to that element’s cascade.

essentialSupport.fact: When CSS does not look right, ask in order: did the stylesheet load, does the selector match, is the declaration valid, and which cascade rule wins? Then inspect layout geometry rather than assuming a computed value guarantees the whole page looks right.

In browser developer tools, the Elements/Inspector style panel shows matched rules and overridden declarations; the Computed panel shows resolved values. Here .notice has greater specificity than p within the same origin/layer/importance, so teal wins even though p comes later. A misspelled class selector would not match at all. This exercise fixes a small selector/cascade problem; it does not automate or replace the developer-tools investigation.

The supplied HTML is separate from the CSS. ```html

``` ```css .notice { color: teal; padding-left: 12px; } p { color: purple; } ```

quizTarget: If the named font cannot load, does the fallback name become useless?
reasoning: A font-family list provides alternatives; loading behavior and resource failure must be considered separately from naming a face.

essentialSupport.fact: @font-face names a font resource that font-family can request. A fallback family remains important while loading or when a resource fails. This tiny original teaching font has only A, B and a space; it is a loading demonstration, not a full reading font or a font-design course.

font-family inside @font-face gives the face its CSS name. src supplies a URL and format hint; url() names the encoded local resource and format("truetype") describes its file format. font-weight and font-style describe which face it is, not an element’s requested appearance. font-display: swap permits fallback text while the face loads. The long data URL is supplied font bytes, not CSS syntax to memorize. The sample rule requests the named face with monospace fallback. Actual loading and glyph width are checked, not merely a family-name string.
Use the supplied original font face for AA with a monospace fallback and swap loading behavior. Keep the supplied encoded resource unchanged.

quizTarget: Would replacing visibility:hidden with opacity:0 reliably disable the first button?
reasoning: Visibility, layout and interaction are separate concerns; use the appropriate semantic control state when disabling an action.

essentialSupport.fact: display: none removes an element’s layout box. visibility: hidden hides it while its layout space remains. opacity: 0 makes it transparent but does not by itself remove its box, pointer hit testing or keyboard focusability.

The two buttons are flex items with fixed widths. Hiding the first with visibility preserves the second button’s position. Changing that declaration to display: none removes its box, so the second moves to the start. Opacity is not a safe shortcut for disabling a control: a transparent control can still act. These properties also differ for accessibility exposure; this geometry exercise is not a complete assistive-technology test.
Hide the first button with visibility while retaining its 100px layout slot.

quizTarget: After removing !important from both declarations, which color wins?
reasoning: Layer priority reverses specifically for important declarations; normal declarations use the ordinary later-layer priority.

essentialSupport.fact: For normal author declarations, later layers outrank earlier layers. For important author declarations, that layer order reverses: an earlier layer outranks a later one. This comparison stays within the same origin and excludes active transitions.

!important is a declaration flag after the value and before the semicolon, not part of the color. @layer base, theme establishes the order before the rules. Both declarations here are important, so base wins even though theme appears later. Removing both flags restores normal layer order and theme wins. User and browser important origins have their own precedence; do not describe this as a universal strongest-rule trick.

Keep the two named layers and make the earlier important base declaration protect the teal text. Supplied checks inspect the authored contract and may temporarily change a value to compare the stated behavior; temporary values are restored. You are writing CSS, not these JavaScript test helpers.

quizTarget: At exactly 600px, does (min-width:600px) match?
reasoning: The min-width condition includes equality. The viewport width is measured in CSS pixels.

essentialSupport.fact: A mobile-first layout starts with a useful narrow arrangement, then adds columns when enough viewport space is available. min-width includes the boundary value and larger widths. This is about available space, not detecting a particular device brand.

The base grid has one flexible column. At 600 CSS pixels or more, the media query replaces it with two equal flexible columns. Keep source order sensible in both arrangements. The preview uses its iframe viewport, not the full app width. A real mobile document also needs the viewport metadata taught in HTML; see the HTML viewport lesson rather than treating CSS as a substitute for that document setting.
Keep one column below 600px and two at or above it, with the same HTML reading order.

quizTarget: Does font:inherit remove the input’s editing behavior or its label association?
reasoning: Presentation and native control semantics are separate. Keep HTML contracts while styling readable controls.

essentialSupport.fact: Native form controls have browser-provided appearances and do not always inherit page typography in the way ordinary text does. Explicit font: inherit can make their text consistent while preserving their native editing and activation behavior.

font: inherit copies the parent’s computed font settings. border-box makes the declared input width include padding and border. min-height reserves room without pretending that one height fits every language or zoom setting. Keep the label association, name and button type in HTML. Do not remove native appearance or focus indicators merely to make the control look like a painted rectangle; appearance can vary across browsers.
Make the named input inherit the form’s 20px text, use a 200px border box, and preserve label and submit-button behavior.
